title: Tune the performance of your medallion pipeline in Fabric Data Warehouse
author: Scirqueira

content.text:
Coauthor - Artur Vieira
Part 5 of a series on medallion architecture with Fabric Data Warehouse
Measure first, then tune the layer that is actually slow
The first four posts covered how to choose a pattern, build the Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers, establish operating rules, and secure each layer for its audience. This final post explains how to identify the source of performance issues and keep pipelines responsive as data volumes and usage grow.
Fabric Data Warehouse manages caching, statistics, compaction, and V-Order by default, so you do not manage indexes or distributions as you would in a traditional warehouse. Effective tuning therefore starts with accurate measurement and workload patterns that allow the engine to operate efficiently.
Use the following layer-by-layer approach to assess performance.
Why this matters
In a medallion pipeline, a slow dashboard is not necessarily caused by the Gold layer. The cause might be a cold cache immediately after a refresh, oversized string columns in Silver, or thousands of small files created by a Bronze load. Identifying the affected layer first helps you focus tuning work where it will improve the user experience.
The layers help here too. Because each one has a single job, each one also has a typical performance lever: ingestion shape in Bronze, data types and statistics in Silver, and table layout and query shape in Gold.
Step 1: Measure before you tune
Start with query insights. Each warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint provides views in the queryinsights schema with 30 days of history. Use exec_requests_history to review individual queries, long_running_queries and frequently_run_queries to identify recurring patterns, and sql_pool_insights to investigate warehouse resource pressure.
Do not judge a query by its first run. The first execution might load data from OneLake into the cache, create statistics, or resume compute resources. Check the data_scanned_remote_storage_mb column: a nonzero value indicates that the query fetched data from OneLake, while zero indicates that the query was served entirely from cache.
Implementation sketch:
SELECT TOP 20 distributed_statement_id, label, command,
data_scanned_remote_storage_mb, data_scanned_memory_mb,
data_scanned_disk_mb, allocated_cpu_time_ms
FROM queryinsights.exec_requests_history
ORDER BY allocated_cpu_time_ms DESC;
Do this well:
• Label pipeline statements by layer, so you can filter query insights for Bronze loads, Silver transforms, and Gold refreshes separately.
• Compare repeat runs, not first runs, before deciding a query is slow.
• Check sql_pool_insights when many queries slow down together. Pressure on the pool is a different problem from one badly written query.
Rule of thumb: if you haven't looked at query insights, you're guessing.
Step 2: Load Bronze in the shape the engine likes
Bronze performance depends largely on how data is ingested. When loading from Azure Data Lake Storage, use COPY INTO and group data into files between 100 MB and 1 GB. If you load multiple Bronze tables, run separate COPY INTO statements in parallel to improve throughput.
Avoid trickle inserts, updates, and deletes. Each small write produces a new Parquet file, which fragments the table and makes later reads slower.
Fabric Data Warehouse compacts small files automatically in the background, but performance can degrade until compaction catches up. Avoid creating unnecessary small files by pre-staging data and loading it in larger operations.
V-Order is another consideration for Bronze. It is enabled by default and can improve read performance with a small ingestion overhead. For a write-heavy staging warehouse, you can disable it. A common pattern uses a staging warehouse with V-Order disabled for raw ingestion and a V-Order-enabled warehouse for Silver and Gold.
Do this well:
• Pre-stage data and insert it in one statement rather than many small ones.
• Keep imported files between 100 MB and 1 GB when possible, and use Parquet instead of CSV for files that will be queried repeatedly.
• Leave V-Order on unless you have tested a write-heavy workload and accept that you can't turn it back on.
Rule of thumb: a Bronze load that creates thousands of tiny files is a Gold performance problem waiting to happen.
Step 3: Give Silver precise types and good statistics
Silver is where you define the data types used by downstream queries, so it is the most efficient place to choose them carefully. Use the smallest varchar(n) that fits the data instead of varchar(8000) or varchar(max). Use integer types for whole numbers when their range is sufficient; a decimal declared without precision becomes decimal(18,0), which can require more storage than an integer type. Use date and time types for temporal values, and declare columns NOT NULL when the model allows it.
Keep data types identical on columns you join or compare. Mismatched types force conversions that cost time on every query.
Fabric Data Warehouse creates and maintains statistics automatically at query time, while proactive refresh attempts to update them after data changes. Because automatic creation occurs during query execution, the first query after a large load can incur that cost. If there is a window between the Silver load and the reporting workload, create or update statistics on columns used in joins, filters, and GROUP BY operations so report users do not experience the additional delay.
Do this well:
• Review column types generated by tools or code-first deployments before they reach Silver.
• Update statistics on key columns after large loads, in the gap before users query.
• Keep transactions short, always COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and add retry with backoff in pipelines to handle transient conflicts.
Rule of thumb: every oversized column in Silver is paid for again in every Gold query.
Step 4: Shape Gold for the queries people actually run
Gold performance improves when queries scan only the data they need. Pre-aggregate recurring business calculations, return only the columns required by the report, and apply filters as early as possible rather than relying on the client to reduce the result set.
For large Gold tables that are repeatedly filtered on the same columns, consider data clustering. You define clustering with CLUSTER BY on up to four columns when you create the table. The engine stores similar rows together, allowing queries to skip files outside the filter range. Data clustering works best on large tables, columns with medium-to-high cardinality, and selective WHERE filters. Equality joins do not benefit, and ingestion requires additional processing because the data is ordered as it lands.
Implementation sketch:
CREATE TABLE Gold.FactSales
WITH (CLUSTER BY (SaleDate, CustomerID))
AS SELECT * FROM Silver.SalesCleaned;
Caching does the rest. In-memory and disk caching are always on and fully managed, so frequently used Gold tables are served from cache after the first read. If an executive dashboard must be fast first thing in the morning, run its key queries after the Gold refresh so the cold start happens before users arrive.
Do this well:
• Choose clustering columns from real filter patterns in query insights, not from guesses.
• Batch Gold refreshes. Clustering works best when DML statements process at least 1 million rows.
• Use zero-copy table clones for development and test copies of Gold tables.
Rule of thumb: Gold should be fast because it's well shaped, not because someone added a hint.
Step 5: Keep it fast over time
Performance isn't a one-off project. Data grows, new reports appear, and yesterday's well-tuned query becomes today's long-running one. Review long_running_queries and frequently_run_queries regularly, and watch sql_pool_insights for periods of pressure.
If you use the hybrid pattern from Part 1, remember that automatic compaction applies to the warehouse, not the Lakehouse. Lakehouse tables accessed through the SQL analytics endpoint still need appropriate maintenance after significant changes. Keep Lakehouse data in the same region as your Fabric capacity to reduce network latency.
Query hints and FORCE DISTRIBUTED PLAN exist for advanced cases. Treat them as the last step, after data types, statistics, layout, and query shape have been checked.
Rule of thumb: tune from evidence in query insights, then measure again.
Performance at a glance
Use this as a quick checklist for each layer.
Layer
Biggest lever
What to check in query insights
Common mistake
Bronze
Batched COPY INTO with files of 100 MB to 1 GB
Load duration by label
Trickle inserts that create small files
Silver
Precise data types and fresh statistics
Long-running transforms and CPU time
varchar(max) columns and mismatched join types
Gold
Pre-aggregation, data clustering, lean queries
Frequently run queries and remote data scanned
SELECT * and judging speed on a cold run
Takeaway
Measure first. Load Bronze in large batches using appropriately sized files. Give Silver precise data types and current statistics. Shape Gold so common queries scan as little data as possible, and use clustering where filter patterns justify it. Continue monitoring query insights because performance changes as data volumes, workloads, and usage patterns evolve.
That closes the series. Choose the pattern by how much Spark you need, give each layer one job, operate it with discipline, secure it for its audience, and tune it from evidence. Do those five things and your medallion architecture on Fabric Data Warehouse stays fast, trusted, and easy to change.
